prize_parts.citation: for discoveries of the physiology of glucagon-like peptide-1 and the incretin effect, and for their translation into long-acting incretin therapies for type 2 diabetes and obesity

statement.case_for: I keep B041 as a single prize part with Drucker, Holst and Knudsen. The round-1 exchange confirmed that all six of us regard the achievement itself as mature and independently confirmed, and the real disagreement is only the third name. My reasoning is that the prize is for an achievement that changed medicine, and the chain has two necessary links: the physiology that made GLP-1 a rational target (Holst in humans, Drucker in proglucagon-derived peptide biology and the therapeutic rationale) and the solution to rapid degradation that made the hormone usable (Knudsen's acylation-based protraction behind liraglutide and semaglutide). Without the second link the physiology would remain a mechanistic finding, and the outcome trials in diabetes, obesity, cardiovascular and renal disease would not exist. A citation worded around physiology and its translation describes these three names without overstating any of them. I do not see a case for a two-part prize this year, because no member proposed one and the second part would have to be a different achievement with its own unresolved credit problem.
statement.case_against: The weakness remains credit. Mojsov's characterization of the active GLP-1(7-36) form is a real contribution, three colleagues name her, and Habener is not on our list, so the supplied record cannot settle priority. Wahren-Herlenius and Sandberg are right that crediting an industrial drug developer next to two physiologists asks one citation to cover two kinds of achievement, and that a reader could call it a prize for a product. I have tested my own position against this and I still hold it, but I hold it with moderate confidence. If the committee decides the prize is for the discovery of the hormone's biology alone, Drucker, Holst and Mojsov is the cleaner basic-science trio and I would not regard that outcome as an error. The cost of my configuration is that it names the less documented discovery question as secondary and the drug step as primary.

responses.point: Wahren-Herlenius would accept Knudsen over Mojsov only if the committee decided the prize is for the therapy rather than the discovery, and wants the Mojsov documentation examined before the choice is closed.
responses.response: I accept the framing, and I am answering it directly. My position is that the achievement is the whole arc, and so the citation names physiology first and translation second, which is the reverse of a prize for a product. I cannot show from the supplied material that Mojsov's contribution was a necessary step that was independent of the Habener group, and a prize should not rest on a priority claim that this committee cannot adjudicate from the record. I agree that the documentation should be examined, and my position would move if that examination showed her identification of the active form to be decisive and uniquely hers. Until it does, I do not think uncertainty about priority is a reason to prefer her over a contribution whose creative and necessary role is not disputed.

responses.point: Linnarsson holds Drucker, Holst and Mojsov with moderate confidence and names Drucker, Holst and Knudsen as the more defensible fallback if the Mojsov priority question cannot be resolved.
responses.response: That fallback is where we end up if the priority question stays open, and I value that you have said so, because it means the real difference between us is small. Your argument that identification of the active form is part of the discovery whereas acylation is engineering is the strongest form of the case against my trio and I have not dismissed it. My answer is that extending the half-life of a peptide with a known short half-life was not a routine step: it needed a creative solution that others had not found, and it is what moved the field from hormone physiology into outcome trials. If you ask me what would change my mind, it is a primary-literature showing that Mojsov's work was the enabling step for the drug design itself, and not only for the biology. Absent that, I would hope you could support the Knudsen configuration in the final ballot.

responses.point: Sandberg asks that, if Mojsov is chosen, the committee state that her inclusion rests on peptide chemistry and characterization and not on first discovery of the hormone, and that the same discipline apply to the drug-centred option, where Mojsov's omission needs an explicit defence.
responses.response: I agree with the discipline you ask for and I apply it to my own trio. If Knudsen is named, the citation must not imply that she discovered the hormone's biology, which is why I keep the physiology clause explicitly credited to the incretin effect and GLP-1 biology and place translation in a separate clause. My explicit defence of leaving Mojsov out is that the record presents her priority as contested and Habener's absence prevents a fair adjudication, whereas Knudsen's role in the drug class is not disputed. I also accept your observation that a two-part prize cannot fit in three names without dropping someone, and it is one reason I do not propose a second part. We differ on whether the prize tradition favors the enabling discovery over the drug design, and I think this is a judgment about this particular chain and not a rule.

responses.point: Perlmann concedes that Drucker, Holst and Mojsov is the cleaner basic-science trio if the discovery strand alone is prize-worthy and would reconsider if Mojsov's contribution proved decisive and independent of Habener, but does not want to split the prize this year.
responses.response: We are close, and I share your view that GLP-1 can carry three names by itself, so I do not propose to split it. You raised a fair question about the newest indications, and I do not think they need to appear in the citation. I deliberately limit the wording to type 2 diabetes and obesity, where the evidence is longest and from large randomized trials, and leave out cardiovascular, renal and neurological claims. I also take your point that optogenetics is a better candidate for a later year than for a shared second part now, and that I should not let familiarity from my own field push it up, so my round-1 alternatives stand and I do not elevate B033.

responses.point: El-Manira finds B033 close to his field but does not push it first because six credited names for three places make any choice contestable and its case rests on a research tool with clinical translation only beginning, and he asks why B004 should rank above B035.
responses.response: I agree with your reasoning on B033 and it is the reason I keep it only as a second alternative. I would add that, for a prize on benefit to human health, the clinical translation question matters more than the originality of the method, and that cannot be answered from familiarity. On your question to Wahren-Herlenius, I still put B035 above B004 as a fallback because it is a new therapeutic modality, but I accept the strength of your point that its credit list omits Eshhar and that Rosenberg is a contested third name. If the committee judged clean attribution to be the decisive criterion for the fallback, B004 would deserve that place, and I would not oppose it. I have kept B035 and B033 as my alternatives because they are the better supported if B041 failed on attribution grounds.

uncertainties: Whether Mojsov's identification of the active GLP-1(7-36) form was necessary, distinct from the Habener group's work, and enabling for the drug design, which the supplied record does not settle.
Whether one citation can credit both the physiology and the drug-design strand with three names without misrepresenting either contribution.
Whether the fallback should be chosen for conceptual novelty (B035, with Eshhar absent and Rosenberg uncertain) or for clean attribution and maturity (B004).
Whether a research-tool method such as B033 meets the criterion of benefit to human health as strongly as a therapy, and which three of six credited names could be defended.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict applies to any shortlisted candidate or credited name. I worked with Paul Greengard as a postdoctoral fellow, and I have co-authored around twenty works with Thomas Perlmann on dopamine neurons, Nurr1 and autophagy, but neither connection touches B041 or the alternatives I name. I am a neurologist and the chair, and I have weighed optogenetics under the shared criteria and not by familiarity. My disclosure is unchanged from round 1.
